title: Reports and exported tables (page 5)
text: Page 5 of the app, Report export, gives you the results to keep: two reports and the tables of the data. Everything on this page uses one final normalization method.

title: Reports and exported tables (page 5)
text:
Final normalization method
Choose the method first; the buttons stay greyed out until you do. Best is the method with the lowest median RSD% among the QC replicates (here Multivariate (PCA)), and each option shows its median RSD%:






Choose another method when, for example, 3.8 shows that it works clearly better for the compounds you are most interested in.

title: Reports and exported tables (page 5)
text:
Reports








Button
Report
For




QC/QA report (html)
the internal report: all quality-control steps, tables and interactive figures, as on pages 2–4 of the app
checking and documenting the processing


Summary report (pdf)
the external report: the project, the methods and the results in a few pages
sharing the results



A progress bar shows how far the report is; the HTML report is shown in the app when it is ready, and Download HTML Report saves it. The reports name the settings that were used, so they document the processing.

title: Reports and exported tables (page 5)
text:
Exported tables
Export data into tables writes five Excel files for the final method (and each of their sheets as a .csv file), ready to download:



File
Content




….norm.xlsx
normalized peak areas of all features (also non-targeted)


….norm_blk.xlsx
the same after blank subtraction


….conc.xlsx
concentrations of the targeted compounds: QCs, study samples and blanks


….conc_all.xlsx
the same with all samples, including the calibration samples


….history.xlsx
what the processing did with each feature and sample (see Processing history)



This is the start of a batch sheet of the concentration table of the example (QuaNTA_example_ESIpos.mvis.conc.xlsx), the feature columns first and then the samples:






How to read it

Sheets: Full has one row per compound over all batches (average and median of the measured values, the curve used per batch); then one sheet per batch with its limits, statistics, model and Notes, the full text of the note icons of table 4.2.
Statistics (minimum, maximum, average, median) use the measured values of the study samples only: values replaced by the LOD/LLOQ rules are left out.
Coloured cells in the sample columns are values that were replaced or are above the ULOQ; the last sheet, Legend, explains the colours:

title: Reports and exported tables (page 5)
text:
Processing history
Some steps of the processing cannot always be done the usual way, for example a batch without blank samples or a compound without a valid calibration curve in its batch. QuaNTA then uses a fallback (e.g. the blank of all batches, or the global curve) and logs it, as it logs every feature and sample it removes. The same log is shown in three places:

In the app, page 1, the tab Processing history next to the processing log: the fallbacks and removals of each step, and the full feature and sample tables in a popup.
In the internal report, section 1.1, the tabs Feature flow (where the features ended), Fallbacks and removals, Feature history and Sample history.
In the exported tables, the file ….history.xlsx (each sheet also as a .csv file).

The feature history of the example (QuaNTA_example_ESIpos.mvis.history.xlsx), a few targeted compounds:






How to read it

One row per feature of the input file, also those removed on the way, with its Status: where it ended (e.g. Quantified, Kept, Removed (blank filter)).
A column per step, in the order of the processing: what the step did with the feature (Passed, Removed and why, Not applied). Empty: the step does not concern the feature, or it was removed before.
Calibration, batch N: the curve used in each batch, its own or the global one, or why the compound was not quantified there.
The sheet Sample history does the same for the samples (outliers, vIS correction, replaced IS zeros, the blank subtracted, the calibration of their batch), and Events lists every logged event, with its kind: removed, fallback, changed (a value replaced) or note.







TipReuse the processing



Save the settings with Download settings (.yml) on page 1. Loading the file later, in the app or with run_quanta.R on the command line, processes new data the same way.

title: Internal standards and outliers (3.1–3.7)
text: The internal standards (IS) are the backbone of the quality control: they are added in the same amount to every sample, so their peak areas should be the same everywhere. Page 3 of the app, Quality control and normalization, first checks them: which ones fail, which samples are outliers, and how stable they are over the run.

title: Internal standards and outliers (3.1–3.7)
text:
3.1 Internal standards
All internal standards with their retention time, m/z, the RSD% of their raw peak areas over all samples, and the number of samples where they were not found (zero). Failed IS are red. In the app, select a row (or use the arrow keys ↑ / ↓) to show that IS in 3.4 and 3.5.












Tip




A low RSD% (e.g. below 20–30%) means the IS was measured consistently; a high RSD% points to drift, matrix effects or injection problems, which normalization should correct.
Zero values are samples where the IS was not found.

title: Internal standards and outliers (3.1–3.7)
text:
3.2 Failed internal standards
An IS fails when more than 10% of the samples have a zero value: it cannot be trusted to normalize the others. Failed IS are removed before normalization. Here 2 of 22 internal standards failed.

title: Internal standards and outliers (3.1–3.7)
text:
3.3 Outlier samples
A sample is an outlier when more than 20% of the internal standards deviate by more than 3 standard deviations from their mean (in log scale): something went wrong with the whole sample, e.g. a wrong injection volume. Outlier samples are removed before normalization (4 here). With the processing option Non-calibration samples only, calibration samples are never removed.












NoteInternal standards not found in a sample



The mean and SD of each IS are taken from its non-zero values, and a zero (the IS was not found in that sample) counts as an outlying IS: a sample that misses many IS is an outlier. After the outlier check, the remaining zeros of the IS are replaced, for the normalization only, by the mean of that IS in the same file type (Sample, QC, Standard or Blank), or by its mean in all samples when it has no value in that file type. The processing history lists every replaced zero.

title: Internal standards and outliers (3.1–3.7)
section: 3.4 Raw RSD% of the selected IS
text:
3.4 Raw RSD% of the selected IS
The RSD% of the raw peak areas of one IS (here Cotinine-13C-d3_IS) within each QC group and each sample class, with the number of samples. The QC groups are replicates of the same material, so their RSD% shows the technical variation alone.

title: Internal standards and outliers (3.1–3.7)
text:
3.5 Distribution of the selected IS
The raw peak areas of the selected IS by sample group (left) and along the injection order (right). Outlier samples are drawn as crosses.












Tip




The boxes should be at the same height in all groups: the IS was added in the same amount everywhere. A group clearly higher or lower suggests a matrix effect in that group.
Along the injection order, the points should form a flat band. A slope or a jump (e.g. at a new batch) is instrument drift, which the normalization corrects.

title: Internal standards and outliers (3.1–3.7)
text:
3.6 Volumetric internal standard
The volumetric IS (vIS) is added to the final extract just before injection; its peak area shows how constant the injected volume was. The bars are its raw peak area in each sample along the injection order; the table gives its RSD% within groups of samples.


















Tip




A flat row of bars and a low RSD% mean a constant volume. Single low bars are samples with less volume (or a failed injection); the processing option Pre-normalize by the volumetric IS corrects for this.

title: Internal standards and outliers (3.1–3.7)
text:
3.7 Internal standards over the sequence
The peak areas of all (non-failed) internal standards per sample along the injection order, stacked, with a LOESS trend of their total. The app has two panels to compare: here the raw values (top) and after the best normalization, Multivariate (PCA) (bottom).
















Tip




Raw: the height of the stacks follows the instrument response; a trend in the LOESS line is drift over the run.
Normalized: the stacks should become even and the trend flat. If they do not, the normalization did not correct the drift well; compare the methods in 3.8.

title: 2. Data overview
text: Data overview is available as the file is read and gives an overview of what is in the data. Can be used to double check that the data was formatted by the app according to your wishes.

title: 2. Data overview
text:
2.1 Samples by category
Every sample by its category (from the File type row) and class. The calibration samples are counted together here; their levels are in 2.2.












Tip




Check the categories: blanks, calibration samples (CalCurve), QCs and study samples (Sample). A QC counted as a study sample, or a blank missing, means a wrong File type in the file.
QC classes are the QC materials; at least two replicates of a class are needed for the RSD% in 3.8 and for choosing the best normalization.

title: 2. Data overview
text:
2.2 Calibration levels
The number of calibration samples per concentration level (read from the names, e.g. Cal0-5 = 0.5), per batch and in total.












Tip




Double-check replicates if they exist in every batch. The LOD/LLOQ method mean + SD needs at least two zero calibrants (Cal0), and the RSD% option at least two replicates of each level; a batch without them uses the curve of all batches together.
A level missing in one batch shortens that batch’s curve.

title: 2. Data overview
text:
2.3 Classes of analytes
The features by their Comment: targeted compounds (Quant), internal standards (IS), the volumetric internal standard (vIS) and non-targeted features. (The app lists Quant\… and IS\… with their class names; they are counted together here.)

title: 2. Data overview
section: 2.4 Features by m/z and retention time
text:
2.4 Features by m/z and retention time
Every feature at its retention time and m/z. After processing, the targeted compounds are coloured by their outcome: Quantified (green), Valid curve, not found in samples (orange), No valid calibration (red), or Removed by the blank filter or the QC RSD% filter (crosses). The internal standards are black diamonds, the volumetric IS a blue one; the non-targeted features (grey) can be switched on in the legend.












Tip




Clusters of compounds that were not quantified in one region (e.g. early retention times) point to a chromatographic or matrix problem there.
Internal standards should cover the retention-time range of the targeted compounds: the Closest RT normalization uses the nearest one.

title: 2. Data overview
text:
2.5 Distribution of m/z
The number of features per m/z, in bins of 0.5. Hover over a bar for its range; drag to zoom.

title: 2. Data overview
text:
2.6 Distribution of intensities
All raw peak areas of all features and samples: in linear scale (left) and in log scale (right, positive values only). The note tells how many values are zero or missing.












Tip




The log panel shows the dynamic range of the data; most peak areas usually span several orders of magnitude.
Many zeros are normal for non-targeted features (not found in every sample), but a large share of zeros in the internal standards fails them (see 3.2).

title: Concentrations (4.6 and 4.7)
text: The last two figures of page 4 show the result: the concentrations of the chosen compound (here 1,3-Di-o-tolylguanidine, batch 1) in all samples, and its stability in the QC samples over the whole run.

title: Concentrations (4.6 and 4.7)
text:
4.6 Concentration per class






A box per class (QCs, study groups, blanks) with the samples as points. The colour of a point tells whether its value was measured or replaced by the LOD/LLOQ rules:








Point
Signal of the sample
Value




dark grey: Measured
at or above the mean signal of the LLOQ level
the calculated concentration


red: Not detected
below the LOD signal
LLOQ / 4


orange: Detected
from the LOD signal to below the LLOQ level
LLOQ / 2


blue: Set to LLOQ
at or above the LLOQ level, but calculated below the LLOQ
the LLOQ



With the processing option Replace values below the LOD/LLOQ unticked, the red and orange values have no number: they are reported as n.d. (not detected) and n.q. (not quantified), left out of the plots and statistics, and their number is given under the title. Use the Linear / Log buttons for the scale.
How to read it

Differences between the study groups are what you are after; the QCs should be tight.
Many replaced values in a group mean the compound is mostly below the LLOQ there; its average is then driven by the replacement values, so look at the measured values only (the exported statistics and report 4.6.1 use measured values only).

title: Concentrations (4.6 and 4.7)
text:
4.7 QC samples in acquisition order






The compound in the QC samples of all batches along the injection order (each batch quantified with its own calibration), a line per QC group. Open points are values replaced by the LOD/LLOQ rules.
How to read it

A flat line per QC group means the whole procedure (normalization, blank subtraction, calibration) gives the same concentration from the start to the end of the run.
A step between batches points to a batch effect in the calibration (e.g. a calibration curve of one batch that differs from the others); compare the batches’ curves in 4.4.
A drift within a batch that normalization did not remove points to a compound that its internal standard does not follow well (see 3.8).

title: Calibration curves (4.4 and 4.5)
text:
For every targeted compound (Quant in the MS-DIAL comment), QuaNTA fits a calibration curve to the calibration samples (Cal… classes) and uses it to turn the signal of every sample into a concentration. Section 4 of the app shows the curves one compound at a time: choose the compound in table 4.2, and figures 4.4 and 4.5 follow.
The examples below show LysoPC(18:1) in batch 1.

title: Calibration curves (4.4 and 4.5)
text:
4.4 The calibration points








Figure 1




Each point is one injection of a calibration sample: its spiked (nominal) concentration on the x axis and its measured signal on the y axis. Points of the same concentration are replicates; with several batches, the symbol tells the batch.
How to read it

Colours tell the role of each level:

Cal0 (red): the zero calibrant. Its signal gives the thresholds of the LOD (3×) and the LLOQ (10×, or the mean plus 3 / 10 standard deviations).
LOD (blue): the lowest level whose mean signal is above the LOD threshold.
Within limits (green): the levels the curve is fitted on, from the LLOQ upwards.
Above the ULOQ (olive): levels in the curve but above its linear range.
Out-of-range (grey): levels not used for the curve.

Shading: dark grey below the LOD, light grey below the LLOQ, and olive above the ULOQ (dashed line), the top of the linear range.
Replicates should lie close together. A level with widely spread replicates is a sign of a pipetting or injection problem; with the RSD% option, the LLOQ level must have an RSD% of at most 20%.

title: Calibration curves (4.4 and 4.5)
text:
4.5 The samples on the curve








Figure 2




The line is the fitted calibration curve (linear-1/x2 for this compound). The black points are the calibration samples, the coloured ones the QCs and the study samples by class, placed at the concentration the curve gives them.
How to read it

Samples in the white area are within the calibration range and quantified.
Samples in the grey areas are below the LLOQ (light) or the LOD (dark). Depending on the setting Replace values below the LOD/LLOQ, their concentrations are replaced (LLOQ/2 or LLOQ/4) or reported as n.q. / n.d..
Samples in the olive area are above the ULOQ: within the curve but above its linear range, or extrapolated above its highest level. Treat these values with care, or dilute and re-measure.
A curve far from its calibration points, or points bending away at the top, suggests that the linear range is shorter than the calibration range; see the notes in table 4.2 and the option Enforce linear range.







TipIn the app



Use the arrow keys ↑ / ↓ in table 4.2 to step through the compounds; both figures follow at once. With the processing option Log scale for calibration curve fitting, both figures have log axes, which show the low concentrations better.

title: Calibration limits (4.1–4.3)
text:
Page 4 of the app, Calibration and quantification, turns the signals of the targeted compounds into concentrations. At the top you choose the normalization method (the best one, Multivariate (PCA), is preselected) and the batch; the tables and figures follow. The examples below show batch 1.
How a calibration curve is made, in short:

title: Calibration limits (4.1–4.3)
text:
4.1 Calibration curve samples






The number of calibration samples per concentration level in the chosen batch: the replicates the curve of this batch is fitted on.

title: Calibration limits (4.1–4.3)
text:
4.2 Calibration curve limits






One row per targeted compound with its limits in the chosen batch. In the app, select a row (or step with the arrow keys ↑ / ↓) to show that compound in figures 4.4–4.7.
How to read it

Calibration: the curve used for the compound in this batch: the batch’s own (Batch), the curve of all batches together (Global, blue rows), or none (red rows).
LOD and LLOQ are calibration levels; values below them are replaced or reported as n.d. / n.q. (see 4.6).
Maximum conc. is the highest level the curve is fitted on; the ULOQ is the top of its linear range. They differ when the top levels bend away from the line and the curve was not cut there (option Enforce linear range). A quadratic curve has no ULOQ.
Notes show an icon per kind of note; hover an icon for the full text:

 No valid curve: No valid curve: e.g. too few levels above the LLOQ, no signal, or R² below the minimum. The row is red.
 Kept although not valid: Kept although not valid (option Keep all calibration curves). The row is orange.
 Global curve used: The batch’s own curve is not valid, or the batch has too few replicates: the global curve is used.
 Linear range (ULOQ): Linear range: levels above the ULOQ, which were cut off or are above the linear range.
 Detection in samples: Detection in the samples: not detected in any study sample, or detected but below the LLOQ (not exported).
 Removed before calibration: Removed before calibration by the blank filter or the QC RSD% filter. The row is grey.


The exported tables have the same notes in full, as text.

title: Calibration limits (4.1–4.3)
text:
4.3 Chemicals with concentrations






The number of compounds per batch with a valid calibration curve and concentrations in the samples. Compounds without any study sample at or above the LLOQ are not quantified and not exported.

title: 1. Input data and processing
text: The start page of QuaNTA where metadata is provided, data is uploaded, read and processed using the settings provided by the user. All settings and metadata can be saved as a parameters file for ease of reprocessing with new settings or same settings for new data.

title: 1. Input data and processing

The feature columns
QuaNTA needs these feature columns (exact names): Alignment ID, Average Rt(min), Average Mz, Metabolite name and Comment. Other columns are ignored.


Naming conventions
The Comment column tells QuaNTA what each feature is:







Comment
Meaning




Quant
a targeted compound, quantified with a calibration curve


Quant\<class>
a targeted compound with a compound class after the backslash, e.g. Quant\ATZ


IS
an isotope-labelled internal standard


IS\<class>
an internal standard with a compound class, e.g. IS\ATZ


vIS

empty or anything else

The calibration samples (File type = Standard) carry their concentration in the sample name, after Cal, with a dash for the decimal point: Cal0 (the zero calibrant), Cal0-005 (0.005), Cal0-5 (0.5), Cal10 (10). QC samples with the same Class are replicates of one QC material; several QC materials (e.g. QC-low, QC-high) are possible.


Example dataset
The example dataset provided with the QuaNTA app is completely synthetic and has 196 targeted compounds, 22 internal standards, 1 volumetric internal standard and 1000 non-targeted features, measured in 299 samples in 3 batches.






WarningCheck before uploading



When you click Process data, QuaNTA lists Comment values that do not follow the conventions (e.g. quant, IS-ATZ) and column names that look like the required ones but are not exact (e.g. Comment2). Values that look like Quant or IS are shown in red: they would be treated as non-targeted. Fix them in MS-DIAL or in the file and upload again.

title: 1. Input data and processing
text:
Uploading and reading
The initial page has 3 sections: Input and metadata, reading and processing data and logs



Starting page of app when opened.



Upload file, read and process

If the user has previously saved a parameters file it contains metadata, processing settings and which dataset was uploaded at the time of saving it.
Otherwise, fill in metadata (optional), choose a .txt, .zip or .gz (containing a .txt file) by clicking “Browse” in lower left corner
Choose whether to process batch-wise or globally and read file by clicking “Read data file”. Section 2 is now viewable.




Example parameters file and data loaded and read.

title: 1. Input data and processing
text:
Processing settings
The settings are grouped as in the app. Hover the ⓘ next to each in the app for the full explanation; options that the data cannot support (e.g. a volumetric IS option without a vIS) are greyed out.








Processing data

Having chosen your processing settings click Process data. A popup will warn you of any problems detected in the raw data.




The popup before processing, with a note on the columns of the example file.



Click Proceed to start. The Processing log on the right shows the progress; when it ends with “Finished.”, pages 3 and 4 show the results.




Processing finished: the processing log on the right.








TipSave your settings

title: QuaNTA tutorial
text:
QuaNTA (Quantitative & Nontargeted Analysis) turns an MS-DIAL alignment file into quality-checked, normalized and calibrated data, with reports and exported tables. This tutorial walks through how to structure your data, upload your data and how to interpret the app’s results one figure at a time: what each figure shows, how to read it, and what to do when something looks wrong.
All figures here are made by QuaNTA itself from the synthetic example dataset in example_data/, processed with the app’s default settings, so they look and behave like the figures in the app. They are interactive: hover over points for details, click legend entries to hide or show groups, and drag to zoom (double-click to zoom out).

title: QuaNTA tutorial
text:
Try it yourself

Open QuaNTA on SciLifeLab Serve, or run it locally (see the README).
Upload QuaNTA_example_ESIpos.zip and example_params.yml from example_data/ and click Read data file, then Process data.
Follow the chapters in the menu; each names the section of the app it explains (e.g. 4.5).







Note



This tutorial matches the QuaNTA version in the same commit of the repository. Older versions of the app may differ.

title: Normalization, filters and blanks (3.8–3.11)
text:
QuaNTA normalizes the peak areas with the internal standards in three ways and keeps all of them:
The method with the lowest median RSD% among the QC replicates is chosen as the default (here Multivariate (PCA)); you can choose another one on pages 4 and 5. After normalization, the blanks are compared with the samples (blank filter) and subtracted.

title: Normalization, filters and blanks (3.8–3.11)
text:
3.8 Comparison of normalization methods






Each line is one targeted compound in one QC group: its RSD% among the QC replicates without normalization (Raw) and with each method. The colour is the method that gave that compound its lowest RSD%.
How to read it

Lines going down from Raw mean that normalization made the QC replicates more alike, as it should.
The colours show which method works best for most compounds; the overall choice is the median in the table above.
Lines going up are compounds that the internal standards do not represent well (e.g. a very different retention time or chemistry).

title: Normalization, filters and blanks (3.8–3.11)
text:
3.9 RSD% values






The RSD% of 3.8 as a table: per compound, QC group and method. Filter by QC group or search a compound in the boxes above the columns.

title: Normalization, filters and blanks (3.8–3.11)
text:
3.10 Removed features






The features removed for the chosen normalization method (here Multivariate (PCA)) and why:

Blank filter: a feature is removed unless its maximum or average signal in the samples is more than 5 × its average signal in the blanks; it is mostly contamination.
QC RSD% filter (optional, off in this example): a feature is removed when its RSD% among the QC replicates is above the limit; it is measured too imprecisely.

Removed targeted compounds are not calibrated; they appear at the end of table 4.2.

title: Normalization, filters and blanks (3.8–3.11)
text:
3.11 Blanks compared to samples












One feature at a time: its normalized signal in the blanks (red) next to the QCs and the study samples, before blank filtering and subtraction. The bars are the group means with their standard deviation, the points the samples; the dashed line is the threshold of the blank filter (5 × the blank mean). The first plot shows a compound the blank filter removed, the second one it kept. In the app, choose Per sample for one bar per injection, and step through the features with the arrow keys ↑ / ↓.
How to read it

Samples far above the threshold: the compound is clearly measured; the blank level is subtracted.
Samples at the level of the blanks: what is measured is mainly contamination from the procedure, and the feature is removed.
High blanks in one batch only point to a contamination in that batch; blank subtraction is done per batch.
